primary_meaning: The “Gospel” primarily means the good news that God’s saving reign has come through Jesus Christ—especially through his death and resurrection—calling people to faith, repentance, forgiveness, and new life.
primary_basis: Mark 1:1, 14–15 — Jesus proclaims the gospel of God and the arrival of God’s kingdom.
Luke 4:18–21 — Jesus identifies his mission with the prophetic proclamation of good news.
Romans 1:1–17 — the gospel concerns God’s Son and is God’s power for salvation to everyone who believes.
1 Corinthians 15:1–5 — Paul summarizes the gospel around Christ’s death for sins, burial, resurrection, and appearances.
Acts 10:36–43 — the apostolic message presents Jesus’ ministry, death, resurrection, lordship, and forgiveness of sins.
Isaiah 52:7 — the Old Testament background connects good news with God’s reign and deliverance.

alternatives.meaning: The announcement of the kingdom or reign of God, with emphasis on God’s victory, restoration, and lordship rather than primarily on an individual plan of salvation.
One of the four canonical written accounts of Jesus’ life, ministry, death, and resurrection: Matthew, Mark, Luke, or John.
The whole body of Christian revelation or teaching, including its ethical demands and pattern of discipleship, rather than only the initial saving proclamation.
A message of liberation and restoration for the poor, oppressed, and marginalized, understood in social as well as spiritual terms.
An eschatological proclamation announcing final judgment, worldwide worship of God, and the imminent consummation of his reign.

notes: There is broad consensus on the core sense of “good news” centered on Jesus Christ and God’s saving reign. However, “Gospel” is primarily a theological and literary term rather than a fixed biblical symbol, and traditions differ over whether its central emphasis is Christ’s saving work, the kingdom of God, personal salvation, ecclesial teaching, or social restoration.
